title: Backtesting, Multiple Testing & Research Integrity
excerpt: A backtest tries a rule on past data, but searching many possibilities can make random patterns look impressive. Learn how data leakage, selection, transaction costs and changing conditions affect historical results, and how to test a claim without reusing the same data as proof.
objectives: Identify data snooping, look-ahead, survivorship and transaction-cost bias in a backtest.
Separate development data from an untouched, time-aware test set and explain why peeking destroys independence.
Quantify multiple testing and selective reporting, then report effect size, uncertainty, costs and practical relevance.
Distinguish historical association and prediction from causality, durable skill and investment advice.

lessons.title: A backtest is a conditional experiment
lessons.body:
A backtest asks what a fully specified rule would have done on a defined historical information set. Freeze the signal, rebalance schedule, universe, prices, corporate-action treatment, benchmark, cash rate and cost assumptions before judging it. A return or Sharpe ratio is an estimate, not a discovered fact: it depends on the period, units, leverage and risk definition. For an illustrative strategy with 12% gross annual return and 4% annual trading costs, net return is 12% − 4% = 8%, before taxes or other frictions. That arithmetic does not prove skill or predict the future. Treat every result as conditional evidence about this rule, data and period.

A useful audit is to write the decision rule as a timeline, not just a formula. Suppose an illustrative monthly strategy buys at the close on January 31 and sells at the close on February 28. If the reported February return uses a price of 105 currency units at the sale and 100 at the purchase, the gross return is (105 − 100) ÷ 100 = 0.05, or 5%. If a 0.4 percentage-point round-trip cost is charged, modeled net return is 5.0 − 0.4 = 4.6%. This calculation assumes prices are executable and the cost is measured in percentage points of capital; it does not establish skill, because one month is noisy and the rule may fail under different liquidity or market conditions. For a fuller treatment, see ‘CFA Institute — Investment Model Validation’ in the linked sources.

Consider an explicitly synthetic development exercise with 20 independent signals, each tested at α = 0.05, when every signal is actually noise. The probability that one specified test avoids a false positive is 1 − 0.05 = 0.95. Therefore, the probability that all 20 avoid one is 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.3585, so the chance of at least one apparently significant result is 1 − 0.3585 = 0.6415, or about 64.2%. The expected number of false positives is 20 × 0.05 = 1.00; that expectation is a count, not a 100% probability of exactly one. If a researcher selects the strongest-looking signal and then presents its development result as if it were a pre-specified test, the selection step has made the reported evidence conditional on a favorable search. A disciplined sequence is to log all 20 trials, choose a rule using development data only, freeze it, and evaluate it once on an untouched later period. The calculation assumes independent tests; correlated signals change the exact probability, but do not make undisclosed searching equivalent to one planned test. These figures are illustrative and synthetic, not observed market evidence.
lessons.takeaway: A backtest evaluates a precisely defined historical rule, not an abstract promise of performance.
lessons.formula: Net return = gross return − fees − slippage − other modeled costs

practice.question: An illustrative strategy earns 10% gross and incurs 1.5% fees plus 2% slippage. What net return is modeled before taxes?
practice.hint: Subtract each cost from the gross return, keeping percentage points consistent.
practice.solution: 10% − 1.5% − 2% = 6.5%. This is modeled historical performance, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Searching creates winners by chance
lessons.body:
Trying many signals, lookback windows, thresholds and portfolio rules creates a selection problem. Even if every candidate has no true edge, the largest observed Sharpe can look impressive by chance. In an illustrative calculation, if each of 100 independent tests has only a 5% chance of a false positive, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95¹⁰⁰ ≈ 99.4%. Real tests may be correlated, so this number is not universal; it demonstrates why the full search family matters. Record every trial, failed idea and selection rule. Do not present the winner as though it were the only hypothesis considered.

Selection becomes clearer if you compare the winner with the search size. Imagine 20 illustrative synthetic strategies, each producing a five-year Sharpe estimate under a true zero-edge process. If one strategy ranks first with Sharpe 0.80 while the median is 0.02, the ranking alone is weak evidence: the researcher selected the maximum, not a randomly named strategy. A simple record might show 20 trials, 1 retained rule, and 19 discarded rules; reporting only the retained rule hides 95% of the search. This example assumes the trials are comparable and their noise is roughly exchangeable; correlated signals change the exact probability calculation. The result does not prove every high Sharpe is false, only that selection must be part of the evidence. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Harvey, Liu & Zhu — …and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, an analyst screens 8 synthetic trading rules on 12 monthly development returns, then locks the rule before opening 12 untouched test returns. The selected rule's development average is +1.5% per month, while the other seven average +0.2%, −0.1%, +0.4%, −0.3%, +0.1%, +0.3% and −0.2%; their mean is 0.057% per month, so the winner is 1.443 percentage points above the non-winner average. That gap is a selection contrast, not an estimate of skill: the winner was chosen because it looked best in the same noisy sample. The correct sequence is to freeze its rule and evaluate the test mean once; if the test mean is −0.4% per month before costs, the development-to-test change is −1.9 percentage points per month (−0.4% − 1.5%), not evidence that the strategy caused losses. Report both means, the eight-rule search, uncertainty, turnover and costs, and treat the test result as conditional on this one split. Repeatedly checking that test set or changing the rule afterward destroys its held-out status; a fresh time-ordered evaluation is then needed.
lessons.takeaway: The more alternatives searched, the more surprising-looking winners noise can produce.
lessons.formula: P(at least one false positive) = 1 − (1 − α)^m for independent tests

practice.question: Using the illustrative independent-test formula with α = 0.05 and m = 10, what is the chance of at least one false positive?
practice.solution: 1 − 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.401, or 40.1%. Independence is only a simplifying assumption.

lessons.title: Use chronology and point-in-time information
lessons.body:
Time order is part of the design. A training period is used to choose features or parameters; a validation period can compare alternatives; a final test period is evaluated once. Rolling or expanding windows better mimic repeated decisions than a random shuffle when regimes evolve. Look-ahead bias occurs when a signal uses a later closing price, revised accounting number or index membership that was unknown on the decision date. Survivorship bias removes failed or delisted assets. Use historical constituents and timestamps where possible, and document missing data. A clean split reduces leakage; it cannot make a poor signal causal or guarantee future performance.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a local employment office designs a rule using information available at each month-end from January 2021 through December 2022: refer a jobseeker to training when the district unemployment rate has risen for two consecutive months. The researcher freezes the rule, uses January 2021–December 2022 as development data, and then evaluates it once on January–December 2023 as the untouched test period. If 120 eligible people receive referrals in the 2023 test period and 72 are employed six months later, the test employment rate is 72 ÷ 120 = 60%. For a comparison, 58 of 110 eligible people not referred are employed, or 52.7%; the raw difference is 7.3 percentage points. This describes predictive performance for this rule and period, not a causal training effect.

The chronological split can show whether a pre-specified rule transports to later observations, but it cannot establish that the referral caused employment, that the association will persist, or that the rule is useful after implementation costs. One essential check is point-in-time availability: verify that every unemployment rate and outcome label existed when the referral decision was made, and inspect performance across months rather than only the average. A common misinterpretation is calling the 7.3-point gap an estimated programme effect; referral recipients may differ systematically from non-recipients. Also, once the 2023 results change the rule, that period is no longer an untouched test. For validation principles, see “CFA Institute — Investment Model Validation” in the linked sources below.

Point-in-time checking can be made concrete with a data-availability ledger. Suppose an illustrative signal is calculated at 10:00 on March 5 using a quarterly earnings figure. The company released the figure at 16:00 on March 5, so that value was unavailable at the decision time and must be excluded or delayed until the next eligible decision. If the corrected ledger leaves 8 of 10 monthly signals unchanged, that is 80% availability, but it does not make the remaining two valid. A clean chronological split requires both dates and an information timestamp, not merely an older file. This assumes release times and revisions can be reconstructed accurately; missing timestamps limit the conclusion. A valid timing audit supports honest prediction assessment, not a causal claim or future guarantee. For a fuller treatment, see ‘CFA Institute — Investment Model Validation’ in the linked sources.

A further chronology trap appears when outcome windows overlap across decision dates. Consider an illustrative synthetic forecasting rule that, on each month-end, predicts whether a small firm’s revenue will fall below a threshold during the following 90 days. A January decision uses only the January information set and covers January–March; the February decision uses February information and covers February–April. These labels share part of the economic period, so their errors need not be independent even though decision dates differ. Suppose a frozen rule makes 12 monthly test predictions, gets 8 correct, and is reported as 8 ÷ 12 = 66.7% accuracy. That arithmetic is valid descriptively, but treating the 12 errors as independent Bernoulli trials can make uncertainty too narrow: one common demand shock may affect several forecasts. A defensible sequence is to (1) freeze features and thresholds before testing, (2) attach each prediction to its decision timestamp and eligible outcome window, (3) report scores by forecast origin, and (4) use a non-overlapping horizon or dependence-robust uncertainty method. The 66.7% remains predictive performance, not a causal revenue effect or a guarantee of future accuracy.
lessons.takeaway: Reconstruct what was knowable and tradable at each date before measuring performance.

practice.question: You tune a threshold after viewing the final 2019–2023 test curve. Is that curve still an untouched test?
practice.hint: Ask whether test information changed a research decision.
practice.solution: No. The test became development data. Use a new untouched period for final evaluation.

lessons.title: P-values need the whole research record
lessons.body:
A p-value is the probability, assuming a specified null model and analysis assumptions, of results at least as extreme as observed; it is not P(H₀ true), nor the probability that a strategy works. ASA principles emphasize context, transparency and reporting estimates with uncertainty rather than treating a threshold as a verdict. A p = 0.03 result can be small under one pre-specified test yet much less persuasive after dozens of windows or signals were tried. Pre-registration where feasible, versioned code, complete trial disclosure and multiplicity methods make the evidential claim more honest. The Beyond Statistical Significance theme means report effect size, interval estimates, power and practical costs too.

Consider an illustrative synthetic study that reports p = 0.04 for one pre-specified association. Under its null model, 0.04 means results this extreme or more would occur 4% of the time in repeated samples if the null and assumptions were true; it does not mean there is a 96% chance the claim is true. Now suppose 10 outcomes were examined and the smallest p-value was 0.04. A rough Bonferroni comparison uses 0.05 ÷ 10 = 0.005, so 0.04 would not pass that familywise threshold. The adjustment is not automatically exact when tests are dependent, and a non-passing result does not prove no effect. Report the estimate, units, interval, search record and practical importance alongside the p-value. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on P-values’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst runs 20 independent, illustrative synthetic tests of whether different portfolio rules predict next-month excess return, with every null hypothesis actually true. At a per-test threshold of α = 0.05, the expected number of false rejections is mα = 20 × 0.05 = 1.00, but the probability of at least one false rejection is 1 − (1 − α)^m = 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 0.6415, or 64.2%. Those are different summaries: “about one expected false positive” is not the same as “a 64.2% chance that this family contains at least one.” If the smallest reported p-value is 0.012, a simple Bonferroni screen compares it with 0.05/20 = 0.0025, so it does not meet that familywise-error criterion. The next step is not to relabel the result as proof of no predictability; record all 20 estimates, their uncertainty intervals, the selection rule, and costs, then evaluate a genuinely untouched time-ordered test set. Independence is an assumption here, not a property created by the formula; overlapping signals or repeated tuning can make the calculation inappropriate, while leakage remains a separate design failure.
lessons.takeaway: A p-value is model-conditional evidence; it cannot replace design, effect size, transparency or practical judgment.
lessons.formula: p = P(data at least this extreme | H₀ and assumptions)

lessons.title: Validate, stress and account for multiplicity
lessons.body:
Validation should test whether a selected rule remains credible under changes that were planned in advance. Compare untouched results with realistic fees, turnover limits, latency, liquidity and benchmark definitions. Stress assumptions such as signal delay or doubled costs, and report the distribution of outcomes rather than only the best path. Bonferroni controls family-wise error conservatively for a defined family; false-discovery-rate procedures target the expected proportion of false discoveries among rejected hypotheses. Neither correction repairs bad timestamps, survivorship, dependent observations or undisclosed searches. In an illustrative family of 100 tests, a Bonferroni threshold for overall α = 0.05 is 0.05/100 = 0.0005.

Stress testing asks whether a conclusion survives plausible implementation changes chosen before inspection. Suppose an illustrative strategy earns 6.0% annual gross return with 1.0% annual fees and 1.5% annual slippage. Baseline net return is 6.0 − 1.0 − 1.5 = 3.5% per year. If slippage doubles to 3.0 percentage points, stressed net return is 6.0 − 1.0 − 3.0 = 2.0% per year, a decline of 1.5 percentage points, not 1.5 percent. This assumes costs scale as modeled and ignores taxes, market impact beyond slippage, and uncertainty in the return estimate. A surviving positive result is not proof of robustness, especially after an undisclosed search. Multiplicity control and stress testing answer different questions and should be reported separately. For a fuller treatment, see ‘UC Berkeley STAT C141 — Multiple Hypothesis Testing and False Discovery Rate Notes’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst screens 40 independent, purely null strategy rules in a synthetic exercise, each at α = 0.05, and promotes whichever rule looks best on the development period. The chance that at least one rule produces p < 0.05 is 1 − (1 − 0.05)^40 = 1 − 0.95^40 ≈ 0.871, or 87.1%; the expected number of false positives is 40 × 0.05 = 2.00. A pre-declared Bonferroni screen would instead require p < 0.05/40 = 0.00125 for that family, though dependence among rules changes how the guarantee should be interpreted. The practical workflow is therefore: freeze the 40-rule family, apply the stated threshold without choosing a favorable variant afterward, record every result, and evaluate the selected rule once on an untouched later time block. If the test block is consulted to alter the rule, its independence is gone and it becomes development data. Even a clean test result remains conditional on the simulated null process, timestamp discipline, cost model and the chosen error criterion; it is evidence about this validation procedure, not proof of a persistent market edge or causal mechanism.
lessons.takeaway: Multiplicity tools address a defined error problem; they do not substitute for clean data and honest validation.
lessons.formula: Bonferroni per-test threshold = familywise α / number of tests

lessons.title: Make modest, reproducible claims
lessons.body:
A credible report separates association, prediction, causality, uncertainty and practical importance. An out-of-sample excess return is evidence about predictive performance for a specified historical setup; it is not proof that a signal causes returns or that skill will persist. Show point estimates and intervals, drawdowns, turnover, capacity, benchmark choice, missingness and all material deviations from the plan. Reproduce results from versioned data and code, and label simulated numbers as simulated. A strategy with a 0.20 Sharpe and a wide interval may be less useful than a smaller, more stable effect after costs. No backtest establishes a personal investment recommendation.

Reproducibility benefits from a result table that another analyst can rebuild. For an illustrative synthetic test, a rule earns 4.0% per year before costs, incurs 1.2 percentage points of fees and 0.8 percentage points of slippage, and therefore earns 4.0 − 1.2 − 0.8 = 2.0% net per year. A report should identify the currency basis, annualization convention, sample dates, missing observations, code version and whether the 4.0% is simulated. If a later rerun gives 1.6% after a timestamp correction, the difference is a data-quality finding, not evidence of a causal change in markets. Reproducibility can reveal sensitivity, but it cannot turn association into causation or guarantee persistence. Practical usefulness also depends on capacity, risk and the reader’s circumstances. For a fuller treatment, see ‘CFA Institute — Investment Model Validation’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst chooses one rule on development data and then evaluates it once on an untouched, synthetic 12-month test period. Imagine the selected rule’s mean monthly excess return is 1.2 percentage points and the test-period sample SD is 4.0 pp/month; these numbers are illustrative, not observed market data. Under a simple independence approximation, the standard error is 4.0/√12 = 1.155 pp/month, so a rough 95% interval is 1.2 ± 1.96(1.155) = [−1.06, 3.46] pp/month. Now suppose implementation costs are 0.6 pp/month, treated here as a stated synthetic cost assumption. Subtracting that fixed amount gives a net estimate of 0.6 pp/month and shifts the interval to [−1.66, 2.86] pp/month; it does not narrow uncertainty. The interval includes zero, so the test result is compatible with no net average excess return under this model. Before claiming durability, check whether monthly returns are serially dependent or costs vary with turnover; if so, the simple SD/√n calculation is optimistic and a time-aware or block-resampling analysis is more appropriate. Because the test was used only once, preserve it for future confirmation rather than tuning to this interval.
lessons.takeaway: Transparency and calibrated uncertainty turn a performance story into an auditable research claim.

caseStudy: The interactive chart implements only the independent-null-test calculation described below; the broader research workflow here is a proposed case-study plan, not a set of lab controls. Consider a deliberately illustrative research lab, not a historical dataset: generate a fixed simulated market series and 100 noise signals, split the timeline into development and untouched test periods, and select the signal with the highest development Sharpe. Because all signals are noise by construction, the selected winner demonstrates selection effects rather than investment skill. First run the experiment with point-in-time signals and no costs; then introduce a one-day look-ahead, remove assets that would have failed, and subtract 3 percentage points for turnover costs. Compare the winner's development and test returns, drawdown, turnover and uncertainty interval, and reveal all 100 trials rather than only the winner. A Bonferroni or false-discovery-rate display can illustrate error-control goals, but neither fixes leakage or a misspecified simulator. The exercise supports a claim about how a research process behaves under stated assumptions. It does not estimate a real market edge, establish causality, guarantee persistence, or provide investment advice.
misconceptions: p<0.05 after a broad undisclosed search has the same meaning as a pre-registered single test. Search degrees of freedom change how surprising it is.
A held-out set stays out-of-sample after repeated peeking and tuning. Test information that changes a choice becomes development information.
Multiple-testing corrections fix look-ahead, survivorship and poor data. They address a specified error criterion, not every bias.
A high out-of-sample Sharpe proves causality, durable skill or usefulness. It remains conditional on design, period, costs and uncertainty.
A non-significant result proves no edge. It may reflect low power, noisy returns or a small effect.

quiz.question: After you repeatedly inspect and tune a supposedly held-out period, what is it now?
options: Part of the development process and no longer an independent final test.
quiz.explanation: Repeated peeking uses test information to make choices, weakening its independence. A fresh untouched period or new data is needed for final evaluation.
